A2 Part 3 - Cardio Risk Factors

Author

Ihina, Nikhita, Rishi

Dataset: Cardio Risk Factors

Data Dictionary

Variable Description (Cardiovascular Risk Context) Typical Units / Notes
age Age of the individual; risk generally increases with age years
bmi Body Mass Index; higher BMI is a risk factor for heart disease kg/m²
waisthip Waist-to-hip ratio; central obesity increases cardiovascular risk ratio (waist ÷ hip)
smok Smoking status; major modifiable risk factor 0 = non-smoker, 1 = smoker (or categorical)
choles Total cholesterol; elevated levels linked to atherosclerosis mg/dL or mmol/L
trig Triglycerides; high levels can contribute to heart disease mg/dL or mmol/L
hdl High-density lipoprotein (“good cholesterol”); protective against heart disease mg/dL or mmol/L
ldl Low-density lipoprotein (“bad cholesterol”); high levels increase risk mg/dL or mmol/L
sys Systolic blood pressure; high values = hypertension risk mmHg
dia Diastolic blood pressure; high values = hypertension risk mmHg
uric Uric acid level; elevated levels can be associated with cardiovascular disease mg/dL or µmol/L
sex Biological sex; men and women have different risk profiles 0 = female, 1 = male
alco Alcohol consumption; excessive intake increases risk units/week or categorical (yes/no)
apoa Apolipoprotein A; component of HDL, protective against heart disease mg/dL

In most cardiovascular disease datasets sex is a binary variable coded as 0 and 1, usually, 0 is the reference category and 1 represents the comparison group.

Women are frequently used as the baseline in cardiovascular research because males tend to show higher baseline prevalence and earlier onset of CVD.

Thus we have assumed 0= Female, 1 = Male

Correlation between Age and Cholesterol:

cardio_mod1 %>%
gf_point(choles ~ age, data = cuisines_modified, color = 'maroon', size = 2) %>%
  gf_lm(color = 'black') %>% 
  gf_labs(title = "Correlation Between Age and Cholesterol",
          x = "Age",
          y = "Total Cholesterol")

There is a slight positive correlation between age and cholesterol. More the age, higher the cholesterol. The data also seems to be spread out, great variability.

Age Distribution:

  geom_histogram(fill = "#69b3a2", color = "black", bins = 32) +
  labs(

    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Count of people across ages is fairly distributed.

BMI Distribution by Sex:

ggplot(cardio_mod1, aes(x = factor(sex), y = bmi, fill = factor(sex))) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title = "BMI Distribution by Sex",
    x = "Sex (0 = Female, 1 = Male)",
    y = "Body Mass Index (BMI)"
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  theme_minimal()

According to this graph, females have higher BMI than males, and a more varied distribution + more outliers.

Smoking Status and Sex:

cardio_mod1 %>%
  gf_boxplot(sys ~ smok | sex, orientation = "x", fill = ~factor(sex)) %>%
  gf_labs(
    title = "Blood Pressure by Smoking Status and Sex",
    x = "Smoking Status",
    y = "Systolic BP",
    fill = "Sex: 0 = Female, 1 = Male"
  ) %>% 
  gf_refine(scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Pastel1", direction= -1))

Median Blood Pressure Levels:

  • Female Non-smokers have a slightly higher median (around 130 mmHg) compared to smokers (around 135 mmHg).

  • Males, both non-smokers and smokers have the same median blood pressure (~137-138 mmHg)

Sex difference:

  • Males have higher systolic blood pressure than females across both smoking categories.

  • The distribution patterns are more similar between male groups than between female groups.

The lack of strong smoking effect is surprising, as smoking is typically associated with cardiovascular risks.

cardio_mod1 %>% 
  gf_boxplot(choles ~ factor(smok) | factor(sex),
             fill = ~factor(smok),
             orientation = "x") %>%  
  gf_labs(
    title = "Cholesterol by Smoking Status and Sex",
    x = "Smoking Status",
    y = "Cholesterol Level",
    fill = "Smoking Status"
  )

Median Cholesterol Levels:

  • For females (0): Non-smokers and smokers have almost the same median cholesterol levels (around 5.7)

  • For males (1): Non-smokers have a slightly higher median (around 5.5) compared to smokers (around 5.2

    Distribution:

  • Female non-smokers show greater variability in cholesterol levels with 3 outliers above 10 mg/DL

  • Male non-smokers also display more spread in their data compared to male smokers. Smokers (both sexes) have fewer extreme values

    Sex Differences: Females generally have higher cholesterol levels than males across both smoking categories. Females show more cases of upper outliers. The shorter line (whisker) for female smokers indicates a smaller range of cholesterol values compared to female non-smokers.

Summary:

  • Males demonstrate substantially higher smoking rates than females, while females exhibit elevated BMI, more variable cholesterol distributions, and greater outlier prevalence across multiple health metrics. 

  • Age shows a positive correlation with cholesterol levels. 

  • Males have higher systolic blood pressure overall, though females display more blood pressure outliers. 

  • Surprisingly, smoking status shows minimal impact on blood pressure and cholesterol levels within sex groups, suggesting other factors may play stronger roles in cardiovascular health outcomes. 

  • The age distribution remains fairly uniform across the sample population.
